title: Putting Alcohol-Free Beer on Tap Pays Off for Pubs
paragraphs: Alcohol-free beer has become increasingly popular in recent years, and offering it on tap, rather than only in bottles, appears to be paying off for pubs.

Demand for alcohol-free drinks has grown rapidly. According to the British Beer and Pub Association, no- and low-alcohol beer is now the biggest growth category in the UK beer market, with sales volumes rising by 870% since 2013.

Research suggests that serving alcohol-free beer on draught can make a real difference. In a study published in 2024, researchers from the University of Bristol worked with 14 pubs and bars in Bristol that had never offered alcohol-free beer on tap. When the venues introduced a draught alcohol-free option, their sales of alcoholic draught beer fell by between 4% and 5%. That was equivalent to around 51 fewer pints of alcoholic beer per week for each venue. Importantly, there was no evidence that the change affected the venues' overall revenue.

Pub operators are also reporting positive results. In January 2026, the pub company RedCat described draught alcohol-free beer as a "game-changer," saying it had seen significant growth in sales. It also said that alcohol-free beer served on draught earned higher profit margins than bottled or canned versions.

Large pub groups are seeing similar trends. Stonegate, one of the UK's biggest pub companies, has reported that its sales of low- and no-alcohol beers and ciders rose by 32% in the first quarter of 2025, compared with the same period in 2024.

However, there are still some challenges for smaller pubs. According to the Bristol researchers, one of the main barriers for pubs was cost, since committing to a whole keg of alcohol-free beer, which can cost around £100, often held pubs back.
Nevertheless, the evidence suggests that putting alcohol-free beer on tap can benefit both pubs and public health.
